title: Is the welfare state only for citizens?
subtitle: Algerians and braceros
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: In France and the United States alike, the social protection built after 1945 was also funded by workers from the former colonies. A pension refused to an Algerian, Mexican braceros cut off from retirement, a bulldozer in Vitry: the story of a crisis older than the deficits.
author: mark-n-hoffman

hero.hook: For the workers who came from the former colonies, the crisis of the welfare state did not begin with the deficits: it began on day one.

blocks.text: In **2025**, France's social-security accounts ran a deficit of **21.6 billion euros**. In the United States, the trustees of Social Security, the federal retirement system, project that its reserves will run out in **2034**. For many, the figures prove it: the [[welfare state]], that bundle of pensions, medical care and benefits paid for by taxes, is in crisis.

But a state does not only pay: it also decides who is entitled to what. In 2025, President Donald Trump ordered federal agencies to tighten eligibility checks on unauthorized immigrants, in the name of citizens' pensions and health care. Those immigrants are already barred from most federal benefits. When a government declares a crisis of the welfare state, whose benefits is it talking about?

sections.title: The postwar bargain and its outsiders

blocks.text: After World War II, American manufacturers, unions and the government struck a bargain. Industrial workers won better wages and social benefits; in return, the unions backed mass production and set aside their more radical demands. The political scientist Mark Rupert sees these unions of citizens as the "junior partner" in the arrangement.

blocks.caption: A May 1968 poster from the Beaux-Arts Atelier populaire: the workers of Renault-Billancourt, a major employer of immigrant labor.

blocks.text: France, for its part, built a broader system of public social insurance, funded by both employers and workers; the state has since cut employers' contributions on low wages to encourage hiring. Yet the two bargains share one feature: they favor a national workforce at the expense of non-citizens from the colonies. French factories hire Algerians, colonized yesterday, whom officials now reclassify as "immigrant foreigners." American farms recruit Mexicans whose contracts keep them outside the community of entitled beneficiaries.

sections.title: The Mazari case: a pension refused

blocks.text: In **1986**, Mazari, an Algerian living in mainland France, applied for a supplement to his French disability pension, a benefit reserved for low-income pensioners. The fund refused. A French citizen with the same pension and the same income would have received it: his nationality was the grounds for refusal. In **1991**, the [[Court of Cassation]], the country's highest civil court, struck down that refusal based on nationality.

blocks.caption: The Court of Cassation sits in the Palais de Justice in Paris, on the Île de la Cité.

blocks.text: In **1993**, an influential legislator, Jean Charroppin, echoed a widespread anxiety: claims like these threatened to weigh on France's "social budget." The fear was plain: other immigrants from the former colonies might challenge the same refusals. Yet since the colonial era, the low-paid labor of Algerians has enriched French employers and financed, through taxes and contributions, the welfare state itself. Denying them the rights of citizens amounts to restoring a colonial order.

In the United States, the same logic played out in the fields. The [[Bracero Program]] allowed large growers to recruit Mexican citizens for the harvests on temporary contracts. After **July 1951**, these contract workers were no longer covered by Social Security. Yet Mexico, unlike Algeria under French rule, was an independent country.

American law once barred employers from bringing in foreign workers under contract, seen as a threat to free labor. In 1951, Congress made an exception for the Bracero Program, which already existed: the contracts tied workers to a temporary job and required their return to Mexico.

The historian Mae Ngai calls this an [[imported colonialism]]: Mexican workers entered the American economy without a secure place in the political community, or the retirement and health care promised to citizens as a birthright. The exclusion still applies to farmworkers on H-2A visas, on whose wages employers pay no Social Security tax. Through a variety of legal strategies, France and the United States drew these workers into an imperial workforce while limiting their rights.

sections.title: The "threshold of tolerance" and the Vitry bulldozer

blocks.text: The philosopher [[Étienne Balibar]] examined a widely held conviction: that immigration had crossed a "[[threshold of tolerance]]." Its proponents, on the political right and on the left alike, are quick to blame immigrants for scarce jobs, crowded housing and overstretched hospitals.

In **December 1980**, in Vitry-sur-Seine, the Communist mayor Paul Mercieca sent a bulldozer to block a hostel occupied by Malian workers. [[Georges Marchais]], the leader of the French Communist Party, defended him: Vitry could not take in any more immigrants. There, being French visibly counted for more than being a worker, even among Communists.

blocks.caption: Georges Marchais, general secretary of the French Communist Party, around 1981.

blocks.text: For a long time, France and the United States have recruited workers from their former colonies into their imperial economies. Their labor produced profits and revenue. Welfare rules denied them equal benefits, and when they asked for housing or help, officials counted their claims as new costs. Today's budget warnings come late: for immigrant workers, the welfare state has been in crisis from the beginning.
In France as in the United States, a welfare state funded partly by the labor of Algerians and Mexican braceros denied them equal rights from the start: its crisis did not begin with the deficits.
